title: Uposatha, the moon days
hookLine: keeping the uposatha on each quarter moon for a month
carry: uposatha: a day lived as the awakened live

lines: A DAY AND A NIGHT OF PRECEPTS.
THEN, WHEN THE MOON IS HALF, AGAIN.
cards: Before dawn on a full-moon morning in a Theravada country, people dressed in white walk to the monastery. Some carry food for the monks.
At the hall they kneel, and a monk leads them through the precepts, line by line in Pali, and they repeat after him. Then they stay. They won't eat after midday.
They'll sit, listen to a talk, chant, maybe sleep on a mat on the floor. Tomorrow they go back to ordinary life. A week or so later, when the moon is half, some of them come back.
You met the moon day early on the path. Today, not one moon day, but a whole month of them.

teach.b: The day is called uposatha, an observance day, and it follows the moon: the new moon, the full moon, and the half-moons in between. In the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha describes how a lay follower keeps it.

teach.h: EIGHT PRECEPTS FOR A DAY AND A NIGHT.
teach.b: For one day and one night, they take on eight precepts instead of the usual five. No killing, no stealing. Not just no sexual misconduct, but no sex at all for the day.
No false speech, no intoxicants. And three more: no food after midday; no dancing, music, shows, perfume or jewelry; and no high, luxurious bed.

Each one, the text says, is kept the way the arahants, the fully awakened, keep it all their lives. The lay person says, in effect: for this day and this night, I'll live as they do. A moon day is a borrowed day.
You try on, for one turn of the clock, the life of someone fully free, and then you give it back. Here's why a month matters. One moon day can be a nice experience.
Four in a row, spaced by the moon, start to become a rhythm. Each time, the precepts feel a little more familiar, the hungry evening a little less strange, the quiet a little less loud.

The moon does the remembering for you. You don't have to decide when to practice; you just look up. Across a month, the moon days turn from an event into a calendar, and the calendar quietly turns into a life.

how: In Theravada countries such as Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, devout lay Buddhists keep uposatha days on the new, full and half moons, often wearing white, going to the monastery and taking the eight precepts for a day and a night.

games.q: what does “a month of moon days” mean?
o: a monthly festival to honor the moon as a god
a fast held once a year on the brightest full moon
the observance day kept on the new, full and half moons

p: sets the calendar of the days
keep these precepts all their lives

s: the uposatha comes only once a year
it follows the moon: the new moon, the full moon and the half-moons between.
on the uposatha a lay person keeps eight precepts
for a day and a night: the five, made stricter, plus three more.
the extra precepts include no food after midday
along with no shows or adornments and no high, luxurious bed.

games.q: you keep one uposatha and it was hard: hungry evening, no music, a floor mat. what makes it get easier?
o: skip the next few and try again next year.
keep the next one, and the next, as the moon comes round.
keep all eight precepts forever starting tomorrow.
games.why: the days are spaced by the moon. kept for a month, they stop being an event and become a rhythm.

practice: Bring to mind the shape of the moon tonight; if you don't know it, that's fine.

Picture the coming new moon, full moon and the two half-moons, and next to each, one small thing you might keep that day: no food after midday, no music, a quiet evening, or simply a few minutes of sitting.
Nothing has to be decided now.

wordCard.voice: A month of moon days. Uposatha, the observance day, kept on the new, full and half moons, borrowing for a day and a night the life of the awakened. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali uposatha: the observance day, kept on the new, full and half moons.

carryVoice: Your line: uposatha, a day lived as the awakened live. Whatever its shape tonight, the moon is already keeping count. Same time tomorrow.
